Stated Claim / Post Context:
Latest Bears stadium plan for White Sox site in Bridgeport draws interest — but no involvement from the team

The latest Chicago Bears stadium idea would put the team in Bridgeport, on the site of the White Sox’s Rate Field. But like some of the proposals before it, this one was drawn up without participation from the team.

Actual Article Body:
eNewspaper

Sign up for email newsletters

Sign up for email newsletters

eNewspaper

Trending:

Planners keep drawing new homes for the Chicago Bears, with renderings of football stadiums full of bells and whistles. But a common thread to the proposals is that the Bears aren’t involved.

The latest would put the Bears in Bridgeport, on the site of the White Sox’s Rate Field. But like some of the proposals before it, this one was drawn up without participation from the team. The Bears have said previously that they are focused on pursuing a $2 billion stadium across the state line in Hammond or in suburban Arlington Heights, and that the Rate Field site was unsuitable, citing in part its limited size.

Sterling Bay CEO Andy Gloor made a surprise informal pitch of the plan to Bears President and CEO Kevin Warren, along with Carl Williams, a real estate developer who is the father of Bears star quarterback Caleb Williams, Gloor told the Tribune. But the team said they declined to pursue the plan.

Gloor described the meeting as a casual breakfast encounter rather than a formal presentation, pivoting off his friendship with Carl Williams and Sterling Bay’s work on a potential White Sox relocation to the South Loop. Williams could not immediately be reached on Thursday.

“I’m a huge Bears fan, and I’d love them to stay here (in Chicago),” Gloor said. “I was outlining why it might be a win-win for the Bears. It sounds like they had their minds made up to go elsewhere, but I think it’s a pretty compelling site.”

The proposal, according to a PowerPoint presentation of the plan obtained by the Tribune, calls for the construction of a mixed-use development with a football stadium on the site’s south end. The new stadium could be constructed over land just south of Rate Field while the White Sox keep playing at the current ballpark, until they leave for a proposed South Loop site, according to the presentation.

The renderings also appear to place the new stadium between 37th Street and Pershing Road on the north and south and between the railroad tracks and the Dan Ryan on the west and east, likely displacing much of the Chicago Housing Authority’s 343-unit Wentworth Gardens complex.

The proposal calls for a $5.8 billion initial stadium and campus spread over 200 acres, at least 100 of which would have to be acquired. Funding would depend in part on $1.5 billion in federal rail infrastructure financing, known as RRIF; $400 million in tax increment financing, or TIF; and speculative estimates of $800 million in cash equity from the Bears, $600 million from naming rights and $900 million from personal seat licenses paid by season ticket holders. The plan would also credit the Bears $300 million for their Arlington Heights property.

The PowerPoint plan featured a rendering of a stadium that matched a rendering posted to Instagram by the global architecture firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill on Wednesday. In posting the renderings, the firm described the idea as a “conceptual proposal” of a stadium-anchored mixed-use development that would include housing, entertainment and parks, among other amenities. “Like many in our home city of Chicago, we are eager to enable” the Bears to stay in the city, Skidmore’s Instagram post said.

Sterling Bay did not commission or pay for the stadium renderings, according to the architecture firm, which said it had shared the drawings with a small circle, including Sterling Bay’s Gloor.

Skidmore managing partner Adam Semel emphasized in an interview with the Tribune that the concept was not a formal project, and that SOM itself had not pitched any such project to local officials. SOM also said it has not participated in specific financing discussions.

But he said the firm hoped stakeholders and government officials would be “inspired” by its possibilities, pointing to the success of other sports-anchored districts such as Wrigleyville.

Officials for Mayor Brandon Johnson, who has been overly optimistic about any plan that would keep the Bears in the city, said he was receptive to the idea.

“When stakeholders with a track record of investing in Chicago come to the table with ideas, the Mayor is always willing to meet and listen, as many developers can attest,” mayoral spokesperson Griffin Krueger said in a statement, adding that developers’ ideas “will be vetted thoroughly” and require “community engagement and support.”

“The bottom line is that the Mayor knows that Chicago is and should remain the home of the Bears and will continue to work with stakeholders across the region to make it so,” he said.

The Illinois Sports Facilities Authority owns Rate Field and its surrounding surface parking lots, which means the site is free from property taxes. ISFA CEO Frank Bilecki said Thursday he had not heard from anyone associated with the project.

Team officials have been waiting for state lawmakers to pass legislation that would give them a tax break and money for infrastructure such as utilities and roads. Gov. JB Pritzker has said he supports infrastructure funding but doesn’t want taxpayers to pay for a stadium, a sentiment many fans have shared publicly.

At least one key lawmaker is open to the Bridgeport idea, though he acknowledged several caveats. State Sen. Bill Cunningham, a Chicago Democrat and one of the General Assembly’s lead negotiators on a Bears stadium, called the proposal “very intriguing,” though he said many details would need to be worked out, with significant community input.

Cunningham said he first heard about the concept a couple of years ago through organized labor, when the White Sox were considering building their own stadium on a swath of land known as “The 78,” just south of Roosevelt Road near the Chicago River. In what he called “idle chitchat,” he discussed with a local labor leader whether the Rate Field site, at 35th Street and Shields Avenue just west of the Dan Ryan Expressway, would make a good home for a new Bears stadium.

“I think it’s a legitimate proposal, and one that should be in the mix when it comes to Bears stadium discussions,” Cunningham said. He noted that Rate Field is accessible from the Dan Ryan, the Chicago Transit Authority’s Red and Green lines, and Metra trains.

“It would be way more transit accessible than any other Bears stadium proposal out there by probably a factor of 10,” Cunningham said, adding that much of the land is state-owned. “Ultimately, you know, at the end of the day, it’s up to the Bears. I’ve said this before, what we are committed to is a privately financed stadium.”

The General Assembly adjourned in June without passing legislation aimed at keeping the Bears in Illinois. Two competing proposals each cleared only one chamber.

The House plan, geared toward the Arlington Heights site, would let the team freeze its property tax assessments for 25 to 45 years in exchange for payments to local taxing bodies.

The Senate plan, led by Cunningham, would allow Cook County municipalities with more than 70,000 residents, such as Arlington Heights and Chicago, to create stadium finance authorities. That would let the Bears build on land that is or would become publicly owned, sparing the stadium from property taxes.

“If we are expecting the Bears to pay for the stadium, which we are, then, obviously, the Bears are going to have a lot of say about where the stadium is ultimately located,” Cunningham said.

Indeed, with the fall veto session just weeks away and Bears stadium legislation expected on the agenda, everyone from rank-and-file lawmakers to Pritzker has said it will be up to the Bears to choose where they want to build a new home. And the Bears have given no indication they are interested in Bridgeport. Team officials have said they studied the Rate Field site, along with the former Michael Reese Hospital and South Works steel plant sites, and found none suitable.

In June, the Bears said the team’s board of directors had voted to advance the Hammond project, saying it “will transform the region.” Since then, talks have continued in Illinois, keeping the door open for Arlington Heights.

The White Sox lease at Rate Field runs through 2029, and the Bears’ Soldier Field lease runs through 2033. But the Bears’ timeline hinges more on Indiana, where lawmakers have already approved legislation to finance a stadium through new hotel, food and beverage, and stadium taxes.

Chicago lawmakers are reluctant to help the Bears leave the city, which makes long-shot ideas like the Rate Field plan enticing. The veto session in November and December will be crucial in determining whether Illinois officials can come together on a deal.

In 2024, the Bears proposed building a new stadium on the lakefront to replace Soldier Field, but state leaders said they had no appetite for spending state money to help build it, and the plan was dropped. The team also proposed an enclosed stadium in a mixed-use development on the site of the former Arlington International Racecourse in Arlington Heights, on land it bought for $197 million. Without final passage of the House legislation allowing the team to negotiate property taxes, that plan has also stalled, leaving Indiana as the leading site.

Chicago Tribune’s Brian Rogal contributed to this report.

G-Unit Reeboks Return in White and Green as 50 Cent Sets Date

G-Unit Reeboks are back in white and green. 50 Cent says the G6 retro hits stores 12/14 for $130 after the first pair sold out in under two hours.

Actual Article Body:
50 Cent and the Reebok G-Unit G6 in white and green

50 Cent is dropping more G-Unit Reeboks, and this time the classic G6 is coming back in white and green. Fif shared a first look at the retro on Instagram, telling fans that G-Unit is back on the map and the shoes hit stores on 12/14.

The new pair brings back a colorway from the shoe’s original run in the 2000s. The G6 keeps its clean white leather upper with perforations across the toe and side panels, framed by a cream suede toe cap. Green and white stripes sit along the forefoot, the script “G-Unit” logo is stitched in green on the heel, and green carries through the lining, the outsole and the G6 lace tag. It is the same low top silhouette that took over the streets in 2003, just dressed in green this time.

The White/Green G6 will retail for $130 in unisex sizing through Reebok and select retailers, both online and in stores. Sneaker outlets have confirmed a December release, while 50 himself put the date at December 14.

If the last drop is any indication, fans will need to move fast. Reebok brought the G6 back on August 20 as a faithful retro of the original white, red and blue pair, and it sold out on Reebok.com in under two hours. Inventory at Reebok, JD Sports and Finish Line could not keep up, and the shoes went straight to the resale market.

The sellout gave 50 the perfect opportunity to do what he does best. Rick Ross had predicted nobody would buy the shoes, so once they were gone, 50 hit him with a simple message: “Sold out, fat boy.”

The G-Unit Reeboks have always carried weight beyond sneakers. The G6 first dropped in 2003, the same year 50 released Get Rich or Die Tryin’ and G-Unit put out Beg for Mercy. The shoe went head to head with Jay-Z’s S. Carter line at Reebok, and 50 has long claimed his pair outsold it. He has also said the G-Unit deal with Reebok generated roughly $80 million for him at its peak, proving a rapper could move product like the biggest athletic brands.

Fans who missed the August drop may get a second chance before the green pair arrives, with the original white, red and blue colorway reportedly set to restock in November. Between the restock and a new colorway landing right before the holidays, the G-Unit Reeboks are shaping up to be one of the hottest gifts of the season.

White farmer has his ears hacked off during horrific torture in South African farm robbery: 'The motive clearly isn't just to steal'

A South African man was tortured and had his ears hacked off during a robbery at his farm.

Actual Article Body:
By JAMIE PYATT

Published:  20:16 AEDT, 29 October 2026   |  Updated:  21:33 AEDT, 29 October 2026

A South African man was tortured and had his ears hacked off during a horrific robbery at his farm as the attackers remain at large.

Cattle farmer Donovan Marx, 50, was alone inside his home after his wife Louise had left for work on Wednesday when two men attacked one of his workers in a barn.

The worker was tied up and the robbers then burst into the main farmhouse and shot Mr Marx before stabbing him in the leg.

As he collapsed in a pool of blood, the two men taunted him, held him down and then cut off his ears before slicing them into small bits.

His neighbour said in a social media post that the farmer's employee managed to untie himself and get help – and only a rescuer's arrival thwarted the robbers' threat to castrate Mr Marx.

The robbers did not have time to steal valuables from the farm near Potchefstroom and fled in Mr Marx's station wagon.

He was rushed to the Mediclinic Potchefstroom hospital, where doctors treated his injuries. The hospital said he is 'critical but stable'.

Cattle farmer Donovan Marx was tortured and had his ears hacked off during a robbery at his farm in South Africa on Wednesday

The attackers fled the scene in Mr Marx's station wagon

The victim's brother-in-law Pieter Steyn said: 'Donovan was shot in the shoulder and stabbed in the leg, and we don't know why they tortured him.

'He has not been able to speak to us, and what happened just goes to show once again how brutal farm attacks are in South Africa, and these brutal attacks are out of control.

'The motive clearly isn't just to steal something – it goes further than that.

'The attackers tied up the farm worker, then tortured Donovan, but the worker got free and called for help, which came quickly, and as far as we know the worker is unhurt', he said.

Police arrived at the scene shortly after the attack along with paramedics.

Democratic Alliance MP and Chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Police that oversees the performance of the South African Police Force, Ian Cameron, condemned the attack.

He said: 'Not every farm attack involves torture, but the deliberate cruelty inflicted in some attacks must be confronted honestly, and both these victims deserve proper support.

'I have personally attended scenes after farm attacks where the victims suffered severe torture, such as having boiling water poured over them or poured down their throats.

'People burned with clothing irons or having holes drilled through their hands and feet. Some farm attacks involve prolonged captivity and torture that lasts for many hours.

'The time perpetrators spend with their victims, the severity of the violence and the isolation of the farm properties, all matter when designing an emergency response.

'It is unfair to use comparisons with other violent crimes to trivialise farm attacks and no political leader should welcome or excuse violence against farmers or workers.

'North West Police must ensure experienced detectives investigate this attack and build a case that will withstand scrutiny in court and support the victims.'

North West Police spokesman Captain Majang Skalkie said her officers were still gathering information regarding the horrific attack and would comment further shortly.

No arrests have been made so far, police said.

Dr Corne Mulder, leader of the Right-wing Freedom Front Plus, said: 'The attack on Mr Marx was exceptionally brutal and our prayers go out to him and to his loved ones.

'We repeatedly point out that farm attacks, as in this case, are frequently accompanied by extreme violence and torture and therefore cannot be dismissed as ordinary crime.

'Consequently, our party is again calling on President Cyril Ramaphosa to acknowledge the reality of farm murders and attacks and commit to action that prioritises them.

'As long as this country's president denies the existence of farm murders and refuses to put a stop to incitement of attacks against farmers, then these attacks will continue'.

Dr Mulder said full details of what happened to Mr Marx were too shocking to be made public.

It is the second farm attack in North West Province this week, after a farmer's wife was battered to death with an iron bar as she opened the security gate of their farm at Ottosdal.

Her husband found her in a blood-soaked heap, and she died on her way to hospital.

South African farmers say they believe the government turns a blind eye to crimes against them, which they believe are targeted and deliberately barbaric, yet classify as 'ordinary crime'.

There are between 40 and 72 horrific farm murders a year, which the South African government says is 'not significant' when compared to the 75 murders carried out every single day in South Africa.

But demonstrators claim the barbarity, torture and prolonged suffering that is inflicted on victims of farm attacks means that the crime should be listed as a specific crime.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed a 'white genocide' is taking place in South Africa, alleging white farmers are being targeted and killed and land confiscated.

The US modified its refugee and asylum process to heavily prioritise white South Africans to be able to 'escape persecution' to the US.

South African government officials emphasise high rates of violent crime and farm attacks affect citizens of all races and colour, and there is no targeted white racial genocide.

President Ramaphosa contests strongly that white farmers are singled out for violent attacks.

A social media poster said: 'Donovan is a neighbour and friend of ours and was shot from behind and the round came out his stomach and they cut both his ears off.

'They were picked up at the scene and sent to hospital, but the problem seems to be that they cut them off into small pieces, so they don't know if the ears can be repaired yet.

'They also tried to cut off his genitals, but luckily a worker showed up, and these two pig offspring then made their getaway taking Donovan's farm pick-up to escape.'

In 2021, seven armed attackers ambushed terrified cattle farmer Neil Bierman, 47, and wife Sonja, 43, and their three young sons at their remote farm in Mpumalanga Province.

After forcing them at gunpoint to open a safe and finding no valuables, they forced their six-year-old son into the oven and threatened to roast him alive.

Last year, cattle farmer Role Uys, 70, survived a horrific attack at her farm in Carolina in Mpumalanga Province when a gang held her down as they boiled a kettle of water.

She was tortured for over an hour as they kept laughing and reboiling the kettle to pour over her.

They poured it over her head, then beat her with the kettle, then covered her face in tape, chained her up, and then piled a mound of furniture on her and left her to die.

Incredibly, Ms Uys was discovered alive by callers to the house and survived the torture ordeal despite being critically injured with horrific burns to her head and her face.

The latest Chicago Bears stadium idea would put the team in Bridgeport, on the site of the White Sox’s Rate Field. But like some of the proposals before it, this one was drawn up without participation from the team.

Planners keep drawing new homes for the Chicago Bears, with renderings of football stadiums full of bells and whistles. But a common thread to the proposals is that the Bears aren’t involved.

The latest would put the Bears in Bridgeport, on the site of the White Sox’s Rate Field. But like some of the proposals before it, this one was drawn up without participation from the team. The Bears have said previously that they are focused on pursuing a $2 billion stadium across the state line in Hammond or in suburban Arlington Heights, and that the Rate Field site was unsuitable, citing in part its limited size.

Sterling Bay CEO Andy Gloor made a surprise informal pitch of the plan to Bears President and CEO Kevin Warren, along with Carl Williams, a real estate developer who is the father of Bears star quarterback Caleb Williams, Gloor told the Tribune. But the team said they declined to pursue the plan.

Gloor described the meeting as a casual breakfast encounter rather than a formal presentation, pivoting off his friendship with Carl Williams and Sterling Bay’s work on a potential White Sox relocation to the South Loop. Williams could not immediately be reached on Thursday.

“I’m a huge Bears fan, and I’d love them to stay here (in Chicago),” Gloor said. “I was outlining why it might be a win-win for the Bears. It sounds like they had their minds made up to go elsewhere, but I think it’s a pretty compelling site.”

The proposal, according to a PowerPoint presentation of the plan obtained by the Tribune, calls for the construction of a mixed-use development with a football stadium on the site’s south end. The new stadium could be constructed over land just south of Rate Field while the White Sox keep playing at the current ballpark, until they leave for a proposed South Loop site, according to the presentation.

The renderings also appear to place the new stadium between 37th Street and Pershing Road on the north and south and between the railroad tracks and the Dan Ryan on the west and east, likely displacing much of the Chicago Housing Authority’s 343-unit Wentworth Gardens complex.

The proposal calls for a $5.8 billion initial stadium and campus spread over 200 acres, at least 100 of which would have to be acquired. Funding would depend in part on $1.5 billion in federal rail infrastructure financing, known as RRIF; $400 million in tax increment financing, or TIF; and speculative estimates of $800 million in cash equity from the Bears, $600 million from naming rights and $900 million from personal seat licenses paid by season ticket holders. The plan would also credit the Bears $300 million for their Arlington Heights property.

The PowerPoint plan featured a rendering of a stadium that matched a rendering posted to Instagram by the global architecture firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill on Wednesday. In posting the renderings, the firm described the idea as a “conceptual proposal” of a stadium-anchored mixed-use development that would include housing, entertainment and parks, among other amenities. “Like many in our home city of Chicago, we are eager to enable” the Bears to stay in the city, Skidmore’s Instagram post said.

Sterling Bay did not commission or pay for the stadium renderings, according to the architecture firm, which said it had shared the drawings with a small circle, including Sterling Bay’s Gloor.

Skidmore managing partner Adam Semel emphasized in an interview with the Tribune that the concept was not a formal project, and that SOM itself had not pitched any such project to local officials. SOM also said it has not participated in specific financing discussions.

But he said the firm hoped stakeholders and government officials would be “inspired” by its possibilities, pointing to the success of other sports-anchored districts such as Wrigleyville.

Officials for Mayor Brandon Johnson, who has been overly optimistic about any plan that would keep the Bears in the city, said he was receptive to the idea.

“When stakeholders with a track record of investing in Chicago come to the table with ideas, the Mayor is always willing to meet and listen, as many developers can attest,” mayoral spokesperson Griffin Krueger said in a statement, adding that developers’ ideas “will be vetted thoroughly” and require “community engagement and support.”

“The bottom line is that the Mayor knows that Chicago is and should remain the home of the Bears and will continue to work with stakeholders across the region to make it so,” he said.

The Illinois Sports Facilities Authority owns Rate Field and its surrounding surface parking lots, which means the site is free from property taxes. ISFA CEO Frank Bilecki said Thursday he had not heard from anyone associated with the project.

Team officials have been waiting for state lawmakers to pass legislation that would give them a tax break and money for infrastructure such as utilities and roads. Gov. JB Pritzker has said he supports infrastructure funding but doesn’t want taxpayers to pay for a stadium, a sentiment many fans have shared publicly.

At least one key lawmaker is open to the Bridgeport idea, though he acknowledged several caveats. State Sen. Bill Cunningham, a Chicago Democrat and one of the General Assembly’s lead negotiators on a Bears stadium, called the proposal “very intriguing,” though he said many details would need to be worked out, with significant community input.

Cunningham said he first heard about the concept a couple of years ago through organized labor, when the White Sox were considering building their own stadium on a swath of land known as “The 78,” just south of Roosevelt Road near the Chicago River. In what he called “idle chitchat,” he discussed with a local labor leader whether the Rate Field site, at 35th Street and Shields Avenue just west of the Dan Ryan Expressway, would make a good home for a new Bears stadium.

“I think it’s a legitimate proposal, and one that should be in the mix when it comes to Bears stadium discussions,” Cunningham said. He noted that Rate Field is accessible from the Dan Ryan, the Chicago Transit Authority’s Red and Green lines, and Metra trains.

“It would be way more transit accessible than any other Bears stadium proposal out there by probably a factor of 10,” Cunningham said, adding that much of the land is state-owned. “Ultimately, you know, at the end of the day, it’s up to the Bears. I’ve said this before, what we are committed to is a privately financed stadium.”

The General Assembly adjourned in June without passing legislation aimed at keeping the Bears in Illinois. Two competing proposals each cleared only one chamber.

The House plan, geared toward the Arlington Heights site, would let the team freeze its property tax assessments for 25 to 45 years in exchange for payments to local taxing bodies.

The Senate plan, led by Cunningham, would allow Cook County municipalities with more than 70,000 residents, such as Arlington Heights and Chicago, to create stadium finance authorities. That would let the Bears build on land that is or would become publicly owned, sparing the stadium from property taxes.

“If we are expecting the Bears to pay for the stadium, which we are, then, obviously, the Bears are going to have a lot of say about where the stadium is ultimately located,” Cunningham said.

Indeed, with the fall veto session just weeks away and Bears stadium legislation expected on the agenda, everyone from rank-and-file lawmakers to Pritzker has said it will be up to the Bears to choose where they want to build a new home. And the Bears have given no indication they are interested in Bridgeport. Team officials have said they studied the Rate Field site, along with the former Michael Reese Hospital and South Works steel plant sites, and found none suitable.

In June, the Bears said the team’s board of directors had voted to advance the Hammond project, saying it “will transform the region.” Since then, talks have continued in Illinois, keeping the door open for Arlington Heights.

The White Sox lease at Rate Field runs through 2029, and the Bears’ Soldier Field lease runs through 2033. But the Bears’ timeline hinges more on Indiana, where lawmakers have already approved legislation to finance a stadium through new hotel, food and beverage, and stadium taxes.

Chicago lawmakers are reluctant to help the Bears leave the city, which makes long-shot ideas like the Rate Field plan enticing. The veto session in November and December will be crucial in determining whether Illinois officials can come together on a deal.

In 2024, the Bears proposed building a new stadium on the lakefront to replace Soldier Field, but state leaders said they had no appetite for spending state money to help build it, and the plan was dropped. The team also proposed an enclosed stadium in a mixed-use development on the site of the former Arlington International Racecourse in Arlington Heights, on land it bought for $197 million. Without final passage of the House legislation allowing the team to negotiate property taxes, that plan has also stalled, leaving Indiana as the leading site.

Chicago Tribune’s Brian Rogal contributed to this report.

G-Unit Reeboks Return in White and Green as 50 Cent Sets Date

G-Unit Reeboks are back in white and green. 50 Cent says the G6 retro hits stores 12/14 for $130 after the first pair sold out in under two hours.

Actual Article Body:
50 Cent and the Reebok G-Unit G6 in white and green

50 Cent is dropping more G-Unit Reeboks, and this time the classic G6 is coming back in white and green. Fif shared a first look at the retro on Instagram, telling fans that G-Unit is back on the map and the shoes hit stores on 12/14.

The new pair brings back a colorway from the shoe’s original run in the 2000s. The G6 keeps its clean white leather upper with perforations across the toe and side panels, framed by a cream suede toe cap. Green and white stripes sit along the forefoot, the script “G-Unit” logo is stitched in green on the heel, and green carries through the lining, the outsole and the G6 lace tag. It is the same low top silhouette that took over the streets in 2003, just dressed in green this time.

The White/Green G6 will retail for $130 in unisex sizing through Reebok and select retailers, both online and in stores. Sneaker outlets have confirmed a December release, while 50 himself put the date at December 14.

If the last drop is any indication, fans will need to move fast. Reebok brought the G6 back on August 20 as a faithful retro of the original white, red and blue pair, and it sold out on Reebok.com in under two hours. Inventory at Reebok, JD Sports and Finish Line could not keep up, and the shoes went straight to the resale market.

The sellout gave 50 the perfect opportunity to do what he does best. Rick Ross had predicted nobody would buy the shoes, so once they were gone, 50 hit him with a simple message: “Sold out, fat boy.”

The G-Unit Reeboks have always carried weight beyond sneakers. The G6 first dropped in 2003, the same year 50 released Get Rich or Die Tryin’ and G-Unit put out Beg for Mercy. The shoe went head to head with Jay-Z’s S. Carter line at Reebok, and 50 has long claimed his pair outsold it. He has also said the G-Unit deal with Reebok generated roughly $80 million for him at its peak, proving a rapper could move product like the biggest athletic brands.

Fans who missed the August drop may get a second chance before the green pair arrives, with the original white, red and blue colorway reportedly set to restock in November. Between the restock and a new colorway landing right before the holidays, the G-Unit Reeboks are shaping up to be one of the hottest gifts of the season.

White farmer has his ears hacked off during horrific torture in South African farm robbery: 'The motive clearly isn't just to steal'

A South African man was tortured and had his ears hacked off during a robbery at his farm.

Actual Article Body:
By JAMIE PYATT

Published:  20:16 AEDT, 29 October 2026   |  Updated:  21:33 AEDT, 29 October 2026

A South African man was tortured and had his ears hacked off during a horrific robbery at his farm as the attackers remain at large.

Cattle farmer Donovan Marx, 50, was alone inside his home after his wife Louise had left for work on Wednesday when two men attacked one of his workers in a barn.

The worker was tied up and the robbers then burst into the main farmhouse and shot Mr Marx before stabbing him in the leg.

As he collapsed in a pool of blood, the two men taunted him, held him down and then cut off his ears before slicing them into small bits.

His neighbour said in a social media post that the farmer's employee managed to untie himself and get help – and only a rescuer's arrival thwarted the robbers' threat to castrate Mr Marx.

The robbers did not have time to steal valuables from the farm near Potchefstroom and fled in Mr Marx's station wagon.

He was rushed to the Mediclinic Potchefstroom hospital, where doctors treated his injuries. The hospital said he is 'critical but stable'.

Cattle farmer Donovan Marx was tortured and had his ears hacked off during a robbery at his farm in South Africa on Wednesday

The attackers fled the scene in Mr Marx's station wagon

The victim's brother-in-law Pieter Steyn said: 'Donovan was shot in the shoulder and stabbed in the leg, and we don't know why they tortured him.

'He has not been able to speak to us, and what happened just goes to show once again how brutal farm attacks are in South Africa, and these brutal attacks are out of control.

'The motive clearly isn't just to steal something – it goes further than that.

'The attackers tied up the farm worker, then tortured Donovan, but the worker got free and called for help, which came quickly, and as far as we know the worker is unhurt', he said.

Police arrived at the scene shortly after the attack along with paramedics.

Democratic Alliance MP and Chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on Police that oversees the performance of the South African Police Force, Ian Cameron, condemned the attack.

He said: 'Not every farm attack involves torture, but the deliberate cruelty inflicted in some attacks must be confronted honestly, and both these victims deserve proper support.

'I have personally attended scenes after farm attacks where the victims suffered severe torture, such as having boiling water poured over them or poured down their throats.

'People burned with clothing irons or having holes drilled through their hands and feet. Some farm attacks involve prolonged captivity and torture that lasts for many hours.

'The time perpetrators spend with their victims, the severity of the violence and the isolation of the farm properties, all matter when designing an emergency response.

'It is unfair to use comparisons with other violent crimes to trivialise farm attacks and no political leader should welcome or excuse violence against farmers or workers.

'North West Police must ensure experienced detectives investigate this attack and build a case that will withstand scrutiny in court and support the victims.'

North West Police spokesman Captain Majang Skalkie said her officers were still gathering information regarding the horrific attack and would comment further shortly.

No arrests have been made so far, police said.

Dr Corne Mulder, leader of the Right-wing Freedom Front Plus, said: 'The attack on Mr Marx was exceptionally brutal and our prayers go out to him and to his loved ones.

'We repeatedly point out that farm attacks, as in this case, are frequently accompanied by extreme violence and torture and therefore cannot be dismissed as ordinary crime.

'Consequently, our party is again calling on President Cyril Ramaphosa to acknowledge the reality of farm murders and attacks and commit to action that prioritises them.

'As long as this country's president denies the existence of farm murders and refuses to put a stop to incitement of attacks against farmers, then these attacks will continue'.

Dr Mulder said full details of what happened to Mr Marx were too shocking to be made public.

It is the second farm attack in North West Province this week, after a farmer's wife was battered to death with an iron bar as she opened the security gate of their farm at Ottosdal.

Her husband found her in a blood-soaked heap, and she died on her way to hospital.

South African farmers say they believe the government turns a blind eye to crimes against them, which they believe are targeted and deliberately barbaric, yet classify as 'ordinary crime'.

There are between 40 and 72 horrific farm murders a year, which the South African government says is 'not significant' when compared to the 75 murders carried out every single day in South Africa.

But demonstrators claim the barbarity, torture and prolonged suffering that is inflicted on victims of farm attacks means that the crime should be listed as a specific crime.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed a 'white genocide' is taking place in South Africa, alleging white farmers are being targeted and killed and land confiscated.

The US modified its refugee and asylum process to heavily prioritise white South Africans to be able to 'escape persecution' to the US.

South African government officials emphasise high rates of violent crime and farm attacks affect citizens of all races and colour, and there is no targeted white racial genocide.

President Ramaphosa contests strongly that white farmers are singled out for violent attacks.

A social media poster said: 'Donovan is a neighbour and friend of ours and was shot from behind and the round came out his stomach and they cut both his ears off.

'They were picked up at the scene and sent to hospital, but the problem seems to be that they cut them off into small pieces, so they don't know if the ears can be repaired yet.

'They also tried to cut off his genitals, but luckily a worker showed up, and these two pig offspring then made their getaway taking Donovan's farm pick-up to escape.'

In 2021, seven armed attackers ambushed terrified cattle farmer Neil Bierman, 47, and wife Sonja, 43, and their three young sons at their remote farm in Mpumalanga Province.

After forcing them at gunpoint to open a safe and finding no valuables, they forced their six-year-old son into the oven and threatened to roast him alive.

Last year, cattle farmer Role Uys, 70, survived a horrific attack at her farm in Carolina in Mpumalanga Province when a gang held her down as they boiled a kettle of water.

She was tortured for over an hour as they kept laughing and reboiling the kettle to pour over her.

They poured it over her head, then beat her with the kettle, then covered her face in tape, chained her up, and then piled a mound of furniture on her and left her to die.

Incredibly, Ms Uys was discovered alive by callers to the house and survived the torture ordeal despite being critically injured with horrific burns to her head and her face.
